inputs.root_cause: Applied the same cross-format resource-limit comparison technique that closed the equivalent ora obligation one tick earlier (event 248, SAL-ORA-OBL-1C91BEA24163FEE8): _safe_detached_payload's rule_text (SAL-NRRD-OBL-807586E5B4D0EDB2, NRRD-MULTIFILE-001) explicitly requires 'file count... before allocation' validated for both numbered sequences and LIST payloads. The printf branch already checked file_count against limits.max_entries before building any filename, but the LIST branch built its own names list directly from the header text with no equivalent check.
inputs.obligation_targeted: SAL-NRRD-OBL-807586E5B4D0EDB2 (NRRD-MULTIFILE-001) -- remains partial; evidence strengthened, real bug fixed, no status crossing
inputs.acceptance_evidence: 2 new tests prove: a LIST declaring more names than max_entries is refused before any file is opened; a LIST safely within the limit still loads correctly.
inputs.regression_tier: full nrrd package suite (tests/python/nrrd) plus 6-format regression

execution_steps: 1. After ora's attribute-count gap closed at event 248, checked NRRD's own resource-limit enforcement for the same class of gap, per event 248's own exact_next_action recommending the technique be tried against NRRD next.

2. NRRD's header/payload structure is not a recursive XML tree (confirmed structurally incomparable to ubl/xliff/ora's _Walker/_enforce_tree_limits pattern in an earlier tick), so the direct 4-vector comparison did not transfer. Instead read SAL-NRRD-OBL-807586E5B4D0EDB2's own rule_text directly: 'validate min/max/step/subdimension, filename expansion, file count, and bytes per file before allocation' -- naming file count for BOTH numbered sequences (printf) and LIST payloads.

3. Read _safe_detached_payload directly and found the printf branch already checks file_count = abs(stop-start)//abs(step)+1 against limits.max_entries before building any filename string. The LIST branch builds names = [line.strip() for line in value.splitlines()[1:] if line.strip()] with no equivalent check anywhere.

4. Confirmed this is a genuine, exploitable gap via direct probing before any fix: a NRRD header declaring 200 detached LIST file names (each backed by a real 1-byte file) loaded successfully via load() even with NRRD_DEFAULT_LIMITS.max_entries=64 explicitly configured.

5. Added if len(names) > limits.max_entries: raise ResourceLimitError(...) to the LIST branch immediately after names is built and validated non-empty, matching the printf branch's exact message style ('declares N files, over the limit of M') and its check-before-any-file-is-opened discipline.

6. Re-probed both cases: a 200-name LIST with max_entries=64 is now correctly rejected with 'detached LIST declares 200 files, over the limit of 64'; a 10-name LIST with real backing files still loads correctly and returns the expected array.
7. Ran the full pre-existing nrrd suite (569 tests, zero new fixtures) against the fix to look for false positives before writing a single new test -- all 569 passed unchanged.
8. Wrote 2 formal tests in the existing test_obligation_detached_forms_production.py (extending its established pattern next to the printf sibling test), both passing on the first attempt.

9. Ran ruff (clean), the full nrrd suite (571 passed, was 569, +2), and the full 6-format regression (3442 passed, was 3440, +2; same 4 pre-existing unrelated safetensors interop failures, 2 skipped) confirming zero cross-format regression.

10. Ran skills-first governance: resolve -> add-python-api (COMPOSE_EXISTING_SKILLS), manifest create --write (sfx-3ca8ca9064138402, confirmed as the actually-persisted manifest via ls -t .local/skills-first/manifests/), hand-written receipt YAML, closeout --close -> CLOSE_OK.

11. SAL-NRRD-OBL-807586E5B4D0EDB2 remains status=partial: missing_behavior still lists the multifile writer, the read-time profile gate, the LIST form's own optional <subdim>, and per-file byte validation as genuinely absent -- this tick strengthens evidence with a real, previously-unnoticed exploitable gap fixed, rather than crossing a status boundary.
